analysis.one_liner: Makes mortgage lenders verify borrowers can repay and bans pay structures that reward steering people into costly loans.
analysis.headline: The House passed the mortgage reform bill 300-114 in May 2009, but the Senate Banking Committee never acted on it and it died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, written after the housing crash, would have forced mortgage lenders to verify, with documented income, that a borrower can actually repay a loan before making it. It would have banned bonus payments that reward loan officers for steering borrowers into more expensive loans, restricted balloon payments, prepayment penalties and mandatory arbitration, and given tenants in foreclosed buildings new protections. It also created an Office of Housing Counseling and funded legal help for homeowners facing foreclosure. The House passed it with a large bipartisan vote, but the Senate committee it went to never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Homebuyers and homeowners, especially those offered subprime or high-cost loans, get a lender duty to confirm they can repay and a ban on hidden bonus payments that paid brokers more for worse loans. Refinancing borrowers get a requirement that a new loan provide a net tangible benefit. Renters get protections when their building is foreclosed, and low- and moderate-income homeowners get grant-funded legal help and HUD-certified counseling.

how_it_helps.text: Creditors must make a reasonable, good-faith determination based on verified and documented information that a borrower can repay the loan, its taxes, insurance, and assessments.

Mortgage originators cannot be paid more based on the terms of the loan, banning steering incentives like yield spread premiums, and regulators must bar steering borrowers into loans they cannot repay or that lack a net tangible benefit from refinancing.

The bill restricts prepayment penalties (none at all on non-qualified mortgages, phased out over three years on qualified ones), bars financing single-premium credit insurance, prohibits mandatory arbitration clauses, and restricts negative-amortization loans.
Tenants of foreclosed properties, including Section 8 tenants, receive specified protections, and state attorneys general can enforce them.

HUD must run a grants program providing legal assistance to low- and moderate-income homeowners and tenants on foreclosure, and a new Office of Housing Counseling funds HUD-certified counseling agencies.

Servicers must respond to borrower inquiries within five days, face limits on force-placed insurance, and return leftover escrow balances within 20 business days when a loan is paid off; penalties for disclosure violations are doubled.
Borrowers who were misled gain a defense to foreclosure, because a consumer with a right to rescind a violating loan may assert that right against the foreclosing holder.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage brokers and loan originators lose steering bonuses and face liability of up to three times their compensation for violations. Securitizers must retain at least 5 percent of the credit risk on loans that are not qualified mortgages. Mortgage servicers absorb new escrow, disclosure, and response-time duties with doubled penalties. Subprime and high-cost lenders face bans on balloon payments, loan flipping, and fees, and a counseling prerequisite for high-cost loans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mortgage brokers, securitizers, servicers, subprime lenders

drawbacks.text: The bill limits liability of good-faith assignees and securitizers to rescission and certain costs, bars class actions against them, and lets them avoid liability by curing a violation within 90 days of notice.

The bill preempts state laws that provide additional remedies against assignees, securitizers, or securitization vehicles for ability-to-repay violations, making the federal remedies the sole ones against them for those claims.

A qualified-mortgage safe harbor lets creditors, assignees, and securitizers presume a loan meets the ability-to-repay and net-tangible-benefit standards, weakening the practical force of the core requirement.

A high-cost mortgage cannot be made until a HUD-approved counselor certifies the borrower received counseling, adding a step before credit, and the bill itself directs a GAO study of its effects on the availability and affordability of credit for consumers, small businesses, and homebuyers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary borrowers the bill's core trade is strong: verified ability to repay and a ban on steering bonuses directly attack the practices that produced the foreclosure wave, and tenant and foreclosure-aid provisions help people in crisis. The honest costs fall on industry in compliance and liability, with a real risk that some marginal borrowers lose access to credit, which the bill acknowledges by ordering a GAO study. Its biggest design weakness runs the other way: the liability shields and state-law preemption for assignees and securitizers mean the Wall Street side of the mortgage chain bears much less accountability than the loan officer side. Many of this bill's ideas, including ability-to-repay and risk retention, resurfaced in the 2010 Dodd-Frank law, so the policy itself was not abandoned even as this bill died.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House by a wide bipartisan vote, then sat in the Senate Banking Committee without a markup or vote for the rest of the Congress until it expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Miller (D-NC) introduced the Mortgage Reform and Anti-Predatory Lending Act on March 26, 2009, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee.
The committee held hearings on April 23, marked up the bill on April 29, and ordered it reported amended by a vote of 49-21.
The House passed the bill on May 7, 2009, by a vote of 300-114.
On passage, 240 of 253 House Democrats voted yes and 3 voted no, while 60 of 178 House Republicans voted yes and 111 voted no.
The Senate received the bill on May 12, 2009, and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The bill received no further action in the Senate, and it expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage brokers who earned steering bonuses, subprime lenders, and securitizers kept operating under pre-crisis rules, because the Senate never voted. Homebuyers got nothing from this bill, though many of its ideas were taken up in the 2010 Dodd-Frank law.

sides.party_line_note: House passage split mostly by party: 240 of 253 Democrats voted yes versus 3 no, while 111 of 178 Republicans voted no versus 60 yes, so the bill cleared with substantial but minority Republican support.

industries.note: The bill bans compensation that varies with loan terms, ending steering bonuses like yield spread premiums, and exposes originators to liability of up to three times their compensation. Their gain from steering borrowers into costlier loans was directly the public's loss in the run-up to the foreclosure crisis.

Servicers face limits on force-placed insurance, a five-day deadline to answer borrower inquiries, escrow refunds within 20 business days of payoff, and doubled penalties for disclosure violations. Fee-heavy servicing practices were paid for by struggling borrowers.

The bill bans balloon payments on high-cost loans, restricts loan flipping, caps and phases out prepayment penalties, limits late fees and acceleration, and requires counseling before a high-cost loan. These rules target business models built on repeated fee-generating refinancing of the same homeowners.

The bill hands securitizers significant protection, limiting their liability to rescission, barring class actions, and preempting some state-law remedies, while requiring them to retain at least 5 percent of the credit risk on non-qualified loans and to preserve access to loans in their pools. The liability shield limits homeowner recourse; the retention requirement puts their own money at stake in loan quality.

The bill creates an Office of Housing Counseling and authorizes grants to HUD-approved counseling agencies and state housing finance agencies, with a counseling prerequisite for high-cost mortgages steering borrowers to them. Their funding expands as borrowers get a service they do not pay for directly.

The bill requires a national registry and supervision of appraisal management companies, bars them from having an interest in appraised transactions, and sets registration standards, formalizing an industry it also polices. Appraiser independence rules were meant to stop inflated appraisals that trapped buyers in overpriced loans.
